lesson_title: The Balloon and the Jersey: Charge and Coulomb's Law
hook_text: Rub a balloon on your school jersey and it sticks to the wall. Nothing was glued. So what actually moved?
clip_script: Rub a balloon on your jersey, push it against the wall, let go. It sticks. Nothing was glued, nothing was heated. Here is what happened, and it is the whole topic in one move: electrons got scraped off the jersey onto the balloon. Only the negative bits ever travel — the positives are locked deep inside the atoms and never budge. So the balloon has extra negatives and the jersey is short of them. Nothing was created. Something was moved. That is conservation of charge, right there. But the wall was never rubbed, so why does it hold? Because the balloon's negatives shove the wall's negatives back from the surface, leaving the face of the wall slightly positive — and opposites pull. Same trick as a comb picking up your hair on a dry morning. Now the part that costs marks. How hard do two charges pull? Bigger charges, harder pull, no surprise. But distance gets SQUARED. Move twice as far apart and the force does not halve — it drops to a quarter. Three times as far, a ninth. That is why converting thirty centimetres into 0,30 metres before you square matters so much: get that wrong and you are out by ten thousand.
visual_style: A school corridor: balloon rubbed on a jersey, electrons drawn as small blue dots migrating across, then the wall's surface charges shuffling; the final beat shows two charges sliding apart with a force meter collapsing to a quarter.
mood: Playful classroom experiment turning into a sharp warning.
pacing: Light and quick through the balloon, deliberate slow beat on 'squared', hard stop on the conversion warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never lose a mark to an unsquared distance again.
